name: Bachamal
confidence_why: Ford's 1990 first-hand phonology of Bachamal states that word-accent is predictable, realised as high pitch on the stem-initial syllable and spreading leftward over verb prefixes, and Spencer's 1914 Worgait wordlist independently marks the accent on the first syllable of 20 of 22 words; no source disagrees, but Ford is the only modern description, since Tryon's 1968, 1974 and 1980 work is does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Ford, Lysbeth Julie. 1990. The phonology and morphology of Bachamal (Wogait). MA (sub-)thesis, Australian National University. xii+209 pp. hdl:1885/10815, DOI 10.25911/5d7639ee1d559 (open ANU repository scan with).
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.5 'Word-accent and sentence intonation', (i) Word-accent, thesis pp. 40-41; clitics and compounds pp. 41-43; (ii) Sentence intonation p. 43.
catalog_quote: 2.5 Word-accent and sentence intonation. (i) Word-accent. Word-accent is predictable, the distinction being between accented and unaccented syllables. Accented syllables bear high pitch, unaccented syllables, low pitch. A phonological word is defined as one whose stem-initial syllable is prominent. Prominence is marked by raising the pitch level of the stem-initial syllable of a word, e.g. {tec} ['dɛc] nit, {wara} ['wä$ra] paperbark, {munnuk} ['mʊn$nʊk] toadfish, {warapel} ['wä$ra$βɛl] kangaroo sp., {panpapanpa} ['ban$ba$βan$ba] flat ... {parrkkatta+malaŋ} ['barrk$kat$ta$ma$laŋ] two ... [p. 41] Where the stem-initial syllable is not word-initial, as on verbs, pitch-raising spreads leftwards from the initial syllable of the stem, e.g. {yaŋ+pø+mene} ['yaŋ'$bø$mɛ$nɛ] 1sgA.3sgmO-hit-NF I hit him/it, {pilk+yaŋ+pø+mene} ['bɪlk$'yaŋ$'bø$mɛ$nɛ] slap-1sgA.3sgmO-hit-NF I slap/ped him/it. Inflectional and derivational suffixes are unaccented, e.g. {yaŋaɲ+pø-mene-makka} ['ya$'ŋaɲ$'bø$mɛ$nɛ$mak$ka] 1sgA.3sgfO-hit-NF-PERF I hit her ... {ŋaŋka+pøm+pi+cica+rraŋ} ['ŋaŋ$'ka$'βøm$bi$ji$ja$rraŋ] 1duincS-hug-RECI-HAB we used to hug each other. Clitic and host word form a single phonological unit

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (221 pp., ANU repository scan with scanned layer; bitstream URL in returns HTTP 200 application/pdf, so open access). I extracted pp.52-57 with extracted text and rendered pp.53-54 (thesis pp.40-41) as images and read them directly. Sec. 2.5 'Word-accent and sentence intonation', (i) Word-accent, p.40 reads exactly: 'Word-accent is predictable, the distinction being between accented and unaccented syllables. Accented syllables bear high pitch, unaccented syllables, low pitch. A phonological word is defined as one whose stem-initial syllable is prominent. Prominence is marked by raising the pitch level of the stem-initial syllable of a word, e.g. {tec} ['dEc] nit, {wara} ['wa$r…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (realised as high pitch) is predictable and falls on the stem-initial syllable, which for nominals and other unprefixed words is the word-initial syllable; on prefixed verbs the high pitch extends leftward from the stem-initial syllable over the pronominal prefixes, so the left edge of the word is always high; all suffixes and enclitics are low/unaccented.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; on prefixed verbs Ford marks each syllable from the word start through the stem-initial syllable with the accent mark (leftward pitch spread), not a separate secondary accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Clitic + host and compounds form a single phonological unit (accent on the first element only); word-accent distinguishes a compound nominal ['bam$bac$ka$laŋ] 'woman with baby' from possessive juxtaposition ['bɪ$la$wuk # 'pam$bac] 'Bilawuk's baby'; initial CV of some clitic particles elides after host-final vowel. No lexical exceptions to stem-initial accent are given.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stem + suffixes + enclitics; compounds one unit); accent described in terms of pitch (high vs low), with Ford explicitly separating word-accent from sentence intonation (non-questions end low, questions end high). Examples are citation forms and short inflected verbs.
new_statements.identity_note: Ford describes 'Bachamal' (= Batjamalh/Batyamal), which she states is the name fluent speakers give to the language of the Wajiginy (Wadjiginy) tribe (Ford 1990:4-5); Tryon 1974:206-207 treats Batyamal as a sub-dialect of Wadyiginy sharing 90% cognates with near-identical grammar. Glottolog files both Ford 1990 and Ford 2016 under wadj1254, so no separate glottocode applies. Speakers at Belyuen (Delissaville), Cox Peninsula, NT.

new_statements.quote: p.442: "In all cases the short vowel is indicated by an accent ; when not thus indicated the vowel is long. The syllables on which the accent is laid are indicated by the grave accent." p.485: "The grave accent indicates the accentuated syllable or syllables, and the short vowels are indicated." p.482, Worgait Tribe numerals: "nànji" (one), "bùrkĕta màlung" (two), "bùrkĕtà nànji" (three), "bùrkĕta màlung nànji" (four), "bàquit" (very many). Glossary, Worgait Tribe: "Bàquĕtt" (486), "Bòppa" (486), "Bùlkung" (487), "Delèra" (487), "Kàllum", "Kàllum kundìra" (489), "Kòga" (490), "Kùndein" (492), "Mùragŭll", "Nàmyuk" (496), "Ngùnga", "Ngùngaran", "Ngùrabik" (497), "Wòrgait", "Yărrang mùra" (502).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The two prose quotes are verbatim in the scanned text: p.442 (djvu lines 23946-23949) 'In all cases the short vowel is indicated by an accent; when not thus indicated the vowel is long. The syllables on which the accent is laid are indicated by the grave accent.' and p.485 (lines 27803-27805) 'The grave accent indicates the accentuated syllable or syllables, and the short vowels are indicated.' (differences are scanned double-spacing only). Every Worgait form was checked on page scan (reader's crops in spencer1914_pages/ plus my own 150-dpi renders of pp.113-114, 228-230, 676, 678, 682, 688 and 400-dpi PyMuPDF clips): p.482 numerals nànji / bùrkĕta màlung / bùrkĕtà nànji / bùrkĕta màlung nà…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's Ford 1990 statement (stem-initial accent, high pitch): Spencer's grave falls on the first syllable in 20 of 22 marked Worgait words, and on both words of the compound numerals, matching Ford's {parrkkatta+malang} 'two'. Spencer is a 1912-era lay transcription with no rule statement, so it corroborates rather than refines Ford; Ford 1990:11 herself says 'Bachamal speakers confirm the accuracy of his data'. The two second-syllable marks (Delèra, kundìra) are not explained by Spencer; they would be compatible with Ford's stem-initial rule if those words carry a prefix, but that cannot be checked here (Ford's text has no matching entries for 'arm bands' or 'stron…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Spencer gives no prose statement about Worgait stress; he states an orthographic convention (grave accent = accented syllable; breve/'accent' = short vowel) and applies it to the Worgait words in the numerals table and the glossary. Of 22 distinct Worgait words carrying an accent mark, 20 carry the grave (or the combined short-vowel-plus-grave mark seen in Kŭkka, Nămmŭrung, Yărra) on the first syllable; in the two-word numerals each word is accented on its first syllable (bùrkĕta màlung; Ford 1990 has the same word as the compound {parrkkatta+malang} 'two'). The only non-initial marks are Delèra 'arm bands' and kundìra 'strong' (grave on the second of three syllables) and a second grave on the final syllable of bùrkĕtà in the row for 'three' only.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The preamble allows for 'the accentuated syllable or syllables' (plural) and the two-word numerals carry a grave on each word (bùrkĕta màlung nànji), but Spencer does not distinguish primary from secondary accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Observed non-initial marks: Delèra (p.487), Kàllum kundìra (p.489), and bùrkĕtà in 'three' (p.482, while the same word is bùrkĕta in 'two' and 'four'). Body-text forms on pp.157-162 (kukka, boppa, guga, ngunga, Bidu Bidu, yarra balumna mura, etc.) carry no marks.
new_statements.identity_note: Spencer's 'Worgait Tribe, which inhabits country to the south-west of Darwin' (p.157) is the same people as Ford's Bachamal/Wogait/Wadjiginy: Ford 1990:1 lists 'Worgait' (Spencer 1912:14) among the names for the language, and Ford 1990:11 says Spencer (1914:157-162; 482; 496) marks word-accent and that Bachamal speakers confirm the accuracy of his data. The lexical match is direct: Spencer's 'two' bùrkĕta màlung = Ford's {parrkkatta+malang} ['barrk$kat$ta$ma$laŋ]. Spencer's book covers many tribes; only the entries labelled 'Worgait Tribe' were used.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources. Ford 1990 (catalog) states predictable stem-initial word-accent realised as high pitch; Spencer 1914 has no rule statement but marks the accent (grave) on the first syllable of 20 of 22 distinct Worgait words in his numerals table and glossary (nànji, bùrkĕta màlung, bàquit, Bòppa, Bùlkung, Kàllum, Kòga, Kùndein, Mùragŭll, Nàmyuk, Ngùnga, Ngùngaran, Ngùrabik, Wòrgait, Yărrang mùra..). The residue is two three-syllable words with the grave on the second syllable (Delèra 'arm bands' p.487, kundìra 'strong' p.489) and one row where bùrkĕtà carries an extra final grave (p.482, 'three' only, versus bùrkĕta in 'two' and 'four'); Spencer offers no explanation, and they could be prefixed stems (Ford: accent is stem-initial, not word-initial) or transcription noise. Tryon 1974/1980/1968 (already held by the project from the earlier reading) say nothing about stress.
